e-8674.knowledge_point: Estimating the Value of a Two-Variable Function
e-8674.problem:
Let $f(x,y)$ be a differentiable function such that

$$
f(1,1) = 1, \quad f_x(x,y) = 2xy, \quad f_y(x,y) = x^2.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1),$ estimate the value of $f(1.1, 0.9).$
e-8674.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y) \approx f(a,b) + \nabla f(a,b)\cdot \langle x-a, y-b \rangle.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(1,1)+∇f(1,1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\  & =f(1,1)+⟨{f}_{x}(1,1),{f}_{y}(1,1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\  & =1+⟨{f}_{x}(1,1),{f}_{y}(1,1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find $f_x(1,1)$ and $f_y(1,1)$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =2(1)(1)=2 \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =(1)^{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y) \approx 1 + \langle 2, 1 \rangle \cdot \langle x-1, y-1 \rangle.
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(1.1, 0.9)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x= 1.1$ and $y=0.9,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.1,0.9) & ≈1+⟨2,1⟩\cdot ⟨1.1-1,0.9-1⟩ \\  & =1+⟨2,1⟩\cdot ⟨0.1,-0.1⟩ \\  & =1+0.2-0.1 \\  & =1.1\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
Let $f(x,y)$ be a differentiable function such that

$$
f(1,-1)=-2,\,{f}_{x}(x,y)=2xy-{y}^{2},\,{f}_{y}(x,y)={x}^{2}-2xy.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-1),$ estimate the value of $f(0.95,-1.04).$
after.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(1,-1)+∇f(1,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-(-1)⟩ \\  & ≈f(1,-1)+⟨{f}_{x}(1,-1),{f}_{y}(1,-1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1⟩ \\  & ≈-2+⟨{f}_{x}(1,-1),{f}_{y}(1,-1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{x}(1,-1)$ and ${f}_{y}(1,-1)$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-1) & =2(1)(-1)-(-1)^{2}=-3 \\ {f}_{y}(1,-1) & ={1}^{2}-2(1)(-1)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y)≈-2+⟨-3,3⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1⟩.
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(0.95,-1.04)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=0.95$ and $y=-1.04,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0.95,-1.04) & ≈-2+⟨-3,3⟩\cdot ⟨0.95-1,-1.04+1⟩ \\  & =-2+⟨-3,3⟩\cdot ⟨-0.05,-0.04⟩ \\  & =-2-3(-0.05)+3(-0.04) \\  & =-2+0.15-0.12 \\  & =-1.97\end{aligned}
$$

So, the linear approximation of f at the point (1,−1) is f(x,y)≈f(1,−1)+∇f(1,−1)⋅⟨x−1,y−(−1)⟩≈f(1,−1)+⟨fx(1,−1),fy(1,−1)⟩⋅⟨x−1,y+1⟩≈−2+⟨fx(1,−1),fy(1,−1)⟩⋅⟨x−1,y+1⟩.

Now, we find fx(1,−1) and fy(1,−1) using the given partial derivatives: fx(1,−1)=2(1)(−1)−(−1)2=−3fy(1,−1)=12−2(1)(−1)=3

Therefore, we have f(x,y)≈−2+⟨−3,3⟩⋅⟨x−1,y+1⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Estimating the Value of a Two-Variable Function
content.problem:
Let $f(x,y)$ be a differentiable function such that

$$
f(1,-1)=-2,\,{f}_{x}(x,y)=2xy-{y}^{2},\,{f}_{y}(x,y)={x}^{2}-2xy.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-1),$ estimate the value of $f(0.95,-1.04).$
content.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(1,-1)+∇f(1,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-(-1)⟩ \\  & ≈f(1,-1)+⟨{f}_{x}(1,-1),{f}_{y}(1,-1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1⟩ \\  & ≈-2+⟨{f}_{x}(1,-1),{f}_{y}(1,-1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{x}(1,-1)$ and ${f}_{y}(1,-1)$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-1) & =2(1)(-1)-(-1)^{2}=-3 \\ {f}_{y}(1,-1) & ={1}^{2}-2(1)(-1)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y)≈-2+⟨-3,3⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1⟩.
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(0.95,-1.04)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=0.95$ and $y=-1.04,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0.95,-1.04) & ≈-2+⟨-3,3⟩\cdot ⟨0.95-1,-1.04+1⟩ \\  & =-2+⟨-3,3⟩\cdot ⟨-0.05,-0.04⟩ \\  & =-2-3(-0.05)+3(-0.04) \\  & =-2+0.15-0.12 \\  & =-1.97\end{aligned}
$$
